name: journal-damascus-road-three-versions.json
content:
Paul's conversion is told three times in Acts and once, in a single sentence, by Paul himself. The four tellings do not agree. They differ on who fell down, who heard the voice and who gave the orders, and the man who wrote them down is the same man who was supposed to be keeping the facts straight.

The three tellings in Acts

The first is Luke's own narration. A light from heaven shone around Saul, and "falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?'"1 The Lord told him to enter the city, where "you will be told what you are to do".2 His companions "stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one".3 Ananias then arrived with the commission: "the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road… has sent me so that you may regain your sight".4

The second is Paul speaking to a crowd in Jerusalem. Now the companions "saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me".5 The Greek verb is the one Acts 9:7 uses for hearing, and the King James Version translates the line "heard not the voice". The first telling has the companions hearing. The second has them not hearing.6

[paulus_figure name="lightning-storm-night-sky-8964499"]Lightning over a night sky. Acts describes a light "brighter than the sun" (Acts 26:13).[/paulus_figure]

The third is Paul before King Agrippa. The light is "brighter than the sun", and it shone on Paul and "those who journeyed with me".7 Then: "when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice".8 In the first telling the companions stood. In the third they fell with him.

The orders differ as well. In the first, Saul is sent into Damascus to wait for Ananias. In the third, the Lord gives the whole commission on the road: "I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness", sending him to the Gentiles.9 Ananias has vanished from the story. The goads appear only in the third version.

What Paul says himself

Paul had one chance to tell it in his own hand, in Galatians, and he says almost nothing. God "was pleased to reveal his Son to me", and he "did not immediately consult with anyone".10 There is no light, no voice, no fall, no companions and no Ananias. He went "away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus", and Acts has him instead spending "some days" with the disciples at Damascus.11

One account is vivid and contradicts itself. The other is bare. [paulus_link slug="the-damascus-road" /] goes through the account in full, and [paulus_link slug="saul-the-persecutor" /] asks who Saul was before the road.

What happened next

Acts has Saul led into Damascus blind, healed through Ananias, and baptised: "Then he rose and was baptized".12 Within days "he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, 'He is the Son of God.'"13 Galatians tells the aftermath differently. Paul insists he got his gospel from no human source: "I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ."14

In Acts a human believer lays hands on him, restores his sight and baptises him into the Damascus community. The man who says he learned nothing from men is, in the story that introduces him, healed, told what to do and baptised by them.

Escape from Damascus

The two sources also disagree about why he left. Acts says "the Jews plotted to kill him" and "were watching the gates day and night", and that his disciples lowered him over the wall in a basket.15 Paul tells the same escape in 2 Corinthians and names a different enemy: "the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me".16

Luke has a Jewish plot. Paul has a royal governor. Both end with a man in a basket at a window in the wall, and both cannot be the whole story.

A Muslim reading

In the Qurʾān a prophet brings a message that his people can hear, test and recite for themselves. The Damascus road gives one man a message that no one else heard, and Acts cannot tell it the same way twice. A religion that rests on that event rests on a story its own author never settled.

The verdict

The event on which Christianity rests has one witness. His biographer tells it three ways, and the witness himself, when he wrote it down, left out the light, the voice, the companions and Ananias.

If a court heard these four accounts, it would send the witness away. [paulus_link slug="did-paul-ever-meet-jesus" /] asks what else Paul has to offer, and the answer is nothing that anyone else can check.

The Damascus road: questions readers ask

How many times is Paul's conversion told?

Four times: three times in Acts (chapters 9, 22 and 26) and once, briefly, in Galatians 1:15–17.

Did the men with Paul hear the voice?

Acts 9:7 says they heard it. Acts 22:9 says they did not understand it, from a Greek verb that normally means "hear". Acts 26 says nothing of the companions hearing.

Did Paul's companions fall to the ground?

In Acts 9:7 they stood. In Acts 26:14 Paul says "we had all fallen to the ground".

Does Paul mention Ananias?

Paul never mentions Ananias in any letter or in Acts 26. Ananias belongs to the first two accounts in Acts.
